name: LinkedIn ad sync cookies (UserMatchHistory, AnalyticsSyncHistory, lms_ads, li_sugr, _guid)
plain: Cookies that sync LinkedIn IDs with ad partners and match visitors by probability.
meaning: Keep identifier matches between LinkedIn and ad tech partners. li_sugr (90 days) is a probabilistic match for visitors who are not logged in; _guid (90 days) links to Google Ads.

web.api: Set-Cookie UserMatchHistory, AnalyticsSyncHistory, lms_ads, lms_analytics, li_sugr, _guid, li_giant, ln_or

access.persistence: UserMatchHistory 30 days, AnalyticsSyncHistory 30 days, lms_ads 30 days, lms_analytics 30 days, li_sugr 90 days, _guid 90 days, li_giant 7 days, ln_or 1 day
steps: Ad pixel loads on a partner or LinkedIn page
Partners exchange IDs through redirect syncs

limits.headline: Can match your browser to ad partners' records so ads can follow you
limits.user_action: Nothing. It happens when you visit LinkedIn or a site that uses LinkedIn ads
can: Store IDs in your browser that link LinkedIn with ad partners
Match your visit to ad partner records by probability
Keep the match for weeks or months until the cookie expires
Help show targeted ads on other sites
cannot: Work if you block third party cookies or clear cookies
Know who you are without a LinkedIn login or a match from a partner
See inside other apps or your device
Cross over to a browser or device where the cookie is missing, unless a login links them
limits.differs: Safari and Firefox block many of these cookies by default; Chrome currently allows them unless you choose otherwise.

story.what_it_is: Cookies that help LinkedIn match you with ad partners, even when you are not logged in.
story.for_you: You never see these tiny files. They sit in your browser for about three months and help LinkedIn and ad partners agree that a visitor is the same person. They are why an ad can seem to follow you.
story.for_makers: LinkedIn needs to link its IDs to those of Google and other ad partners to sell and measure ads across sites. A probabilistic match for visitors who are not logged in means it guesses at who you are from device clues. That widens the audience a campaign can reach.

use_cases.example: You read a news site, then see a LinkedIn ad for a tool you looked at, because sync cookies helped match you across sites.
An advertiser sees one person counted across LinkedIn and Google ads, instead of two people, which cleans up reports.
A shopper looked at a pair of shoes at work, and sees a related ad on a LinkedIn feed later that day.
The same ID helps spot one browser acting in ways no real person would, like thousands of page views.
A person plays LinkedIn Games like Queens or Zip logged out, and the ad sync cookies still tag the browser for ad matching.
A publisher with a LinkedIn tag sells its audience to advertisers, using the synced IDs to prove the readers are real.

risks: Guess based matching for logged out visitors
